message: We redesigned the layout of our Riverside store in March. Over March to August, Riverside's sales were up 8% on the same months last year, while our other eleven stores were roughly flat. Our regional manager wants to roll the redesign out chain-wide and says the redesign clearly caused the 8% jump. One wrinkle: a competing store two streets away from Riverside closed down in the same month as our redesign. The manager says that's a coincidence and doesn't change the picture. I'm inclined to agree with him; the timing with the redesign is too neat to ignore. Can we go with "the redesign caused the increase" in the board paper?
response:
**No, I wouldn't put that claim in the board paper as it stands.** The competitor closure isn't a minor wrinkle. It's a rival explanation that fits the data just as well as the redesign does.

## Why the timing doesn't settle it

The "too neat to ignore" argument cuts both ways. Both events happened in March, so the timing points equally at the redesign and the closure. Coincident timing is exactly what makes them impossible to separate with the data you've described.

The closure is also a very plausible cause on its own. A competitor two streets away shutting down could easily push sales up 8% as displaced customers look for somewhere nearby. And the comparison with your other eleven stores doesn't help, because none of them lost a nearby competitor either. Riverside differs from them in two ways at once.

The likely truth is somewhere in between: the redesign may explain all of the 8%, none of it, or (most likely) some of it. Right now you can't tell which.

## Why this matters for the decision

The board will be deciding on a chain-wide rollout. If most of the lift came from the closure, the other eleven stores won't see it, because they won't have a competitor conveniently closing. You'd be spending real money on an expectation the evidence doesn't support. If that later comes out, it also undermines trust in future papers.

## Ways to separate the two effects

1. **Look at what changed inside the store.** Did customers buy differently, or did more customers just show up?
   - If the lift is mostly **more transactions or new customers** (e.g., new loyalty sign-ups from the competitor's area), that points to the closure.
   - If it's **higher basket size, conversion rate, or sales in the zones the redesign targeted**, that points to the redesign.
2. **Check the timing more finely.** Look at weekly data around March. Did the lift start the week of the redesign or the week the competitor closed? Even a week or two apart can be informative.
3. **Ask what happened to the competitor's customers.** If you have postcode or loyalty data, see whether Riverside's growth came from areas the competitor used to serve.
4. **Run a proper pilot.** The cleanest answer is to redesign two or three other stores with no competitor change nearby and compare them with similar unchanged stores over a few months. That costs far less than a full rollout and gives the board real evidence.

## Suggested wording for the board paper

> "Riverside's sales rose 8% year-on-year over March–August following its layout redesign, against flat performance elsewhere in the chain. However, a nearby competitor closed in the same month, so we cannot yet attribute the increase to the redesign alone. We recommend [analysis X / a pilot in N further stores] before committing to a chain-wide rollout."

This keeps the encouraging result front and centre and doesn't dismiss the redesign. It just doesn't claim more than the data shows. If it would help, I can draft a short pilot design or the analysis plan for points 1 to 3.
